**00:02:45–00:02:49** judging or labeling people. And so what we'll do is just give a quick talk about some of those

**00:02:49–00:02:54** features that I may have missed through the webinar and then we're going to press on to

**00:02:54–00:02:58** some other more important take-home. So it's really important for particularly young

**00:02:58–00:03:04** practitioners to reflect on this. Everybody, or lots of people in my experience, tend to verbalize

**00:03:04–00:03:09** that they want to be a high performance manager or they want to be a department lead and all the

**00:03:09–00:03:14** rest of it. Now, leadership is not something you suddenly switch on. You can't just get the job.

**00:03:14–00:03:18** As I used to always say, it's not a badge. You don't even get a badge and suddenly everyone

**00:03:18–00:03:23** listens to you. It's kind of like preschool that type of thing. You've got to practice it.

**00:03:23–00:03:30** You've got to start understanding people. So I always always say to mid-career practitioners,

**00:03:30–00:03:33** people who are saying, I want to aspire to be more. I want to lead a department.

**00:03:33–00:03:38** You've got to start practicing it. And so this is a good opportunity for you to practice it,

**00:03:38–00:03:43** to just start thinking about not only reviewing yourself, but reviewing what's around you. So

**00:03:43–00:03:47** in the webinar, we talked about the knowledge behavior matrix and how it's all set up.

**00:03:47–00:03:51** But let's just go through a couple of the points very, very quickly. Looking about

**00:03:51–00:03:57** reviewing where I'm at and where my staff are at. So it's worthwhile just going through

**00:03:59–00:04:04** a couple of the little pieces within that. On the knowledge side, the handbrake. So that's

**00:04:04–00:04:09** the person who lacks understanding, especially around technology and core concepts. Now they're

**00:04:09–00:04:14** going to slow everything down. And those people may also technically not want to go anywhere.

**00:04:14–00:04:18** Challenge is some of these people don't even know how far behind they are. They think they're on

**00:04:18–00:04:23** top of the world, but they're not. Worst case is they're the folks that don't want to learn. Now,

**00:04:23–00:04:28** I would say that doing things like quizzing your staff intermittently, having conversations,

**00:04:28–00:04:32** hey, what are you working on? What are you working on on your CPD? I'm a big believer in

**00:04:32–00:04:36** people driving what they want to learn and making sure we've got time to do so.

**00:04:36–00:04:40** We'll cover that elsewhere. Asking those sort of folks to present, hey, where are you at? Listen,

**00:04:40–00:04:44** we've got a staff meeting. Just give us 10 minutes of what you've been working on last month.

**00:04:44–00:04:49** Challenging them to bring something to the front to get them out in front of people. Now,

**00:04:49–00:04:52** they're only going to come to the party and list again, or they don't, but it starts to

**00:04:52–00:04:58** show you where they're at. Now, if you've got that plus a bad behavior, so it's going to be a

**00:04:58–00:05:06** big impact on your staff. Risk areas are going to delay, cause frustration. One of the big things

**00:05:06–00:05:12** that blows everybody down and slows senior staff down is the need to have to interpret and work

**00:05:12–00:05:16** with people who can't get on with their own work. Understand that we've got to help people develop.

**00:05:16–00:05:21** 100% behind that. At some point, we need to have people come into a job and be able to do

**00:05:21–00:05:26** excellent work. That brings us to the porn. Yet, I talked about chess. I think it's a great

**00:05:26–00:05:31** idea. Porn is a great piece that can do a lot of really cool things. I can generate an amendment,

**00:05:31–00:05:36** can support people. It's got huge growth potential because as I said in the webinar,

**00:05:36–00:05:40** if you can get to the back rank, you turn into a queen, which is the strongest piece on the board,

**00:05:40–00:05:44** but they need to want to move on. Attitioners are solid professionals where you experience

**00:05:44–00:05:49** basic frameworks, acknowledge they're usually the backbone of your department. They can deliver

**00:05:49–00:05:55** consistently. What we need to know from those folks is can we get them to the next level,

**00:05:59–00:06:05** troubleshoot complex systems, particularly as we know now, tech heavy ones. It's really important

**00:06:05–00:06:10** for aspiring staff to understand where you sit in that because what you're trying to do is then

**00:06:10–00:06:15** define who your mentors are because a mentor needs to be in that top bracket, needs to be

**00:06:15–00:06:20** above you. Now, if you're a handbraker and you're trying to get mentored off a porn,

**00:06:20–00:06:24** probably not ideal, but you want to look to that practitioner and that operator level.

**00:06:24–00:06:29** People have been around, real mentors who've worked at a level, Olympic level, NFL,

**00:06:35–00:06:40** oh, my mentor was Joe Schmoe who had a gym down the road. I'm like, what has he taught you?

**00:06:42–00:06:47** That person doesn't necessarily have any great, we need to know more about Joe Schmoe. If Joe

**00:06:47–00:06:51** Schmoe's never done this, he can in this day and age, we have lots of people coming out of

**00:06:51–00:06:57** university who choose not to go into sport and challenge themselves. They go and do business,

**00:07:07–00:07:13** Because the accountability process, the detail, the timing, the tempo, which we'll talk about more,

**00:07:13–00:07:18** is critically important. Evaluate your mentors in the same way you're evaluating your staff.

**00:00:37–00:00:42** the world, but what actually happens is without discipline, all we end up is with more data,

**00:00:47–00:00:53** way, shape, or form. As the creator of Speed Seek, I know that technology exists as a tool

input.content:
# Module 1: People, Language, and Discipline Before Technology

Module 1 argues that the performance industry has spent the last fifteen years buying technology faster than it has built the people, shared language, and procedures needed to use it. Jason Weber (Old Bull Performance, creator of SpeedSig) traces the field from Milo of Croton to machine learning to show that the constraint is no longer access to information or equipment; it is vetting, filtering, and integrating what you already have. The module's fix has three layers: audit your people on a knowledge and behaviour matrix, agree a common language so cross-discipline staff can locate an athlete and a purpose in seconds, and inventory your tech stack by measurement system so you know what each device actually measures and whether you can repeat the number. The recurring principle is that discipline breeds freedom: standardised procedures produce reliability, reliability produces confidence, and confidence produces decisions you can defend. Every piece of equipment is a tool that must sit inside an operating system; the tool is not the upgrade, the discipline is.

## Lessons

### Webinar 1, Parts I to III: From Milo to Machine Learning (transcript-only, speaker unnamed but consistent with Weber)

- Part I is a history: Milo's calf as progressive overload; 1950s to 1970s birth of modern sport science (USSR institutes, Matveyev's periodisation, Verkhoshansky's shock method, VO2max work); 1970s to 1990s institutes and specialisation (AIS, Ball State biomechanics, Holloszy and Costill); 1990s explosion of injury epidemiology, EMG, 3D motion analysis, plus a second stream of coach-sourced information (Poliquin, King, Chek); 2000 to 2020 the "technology quickening" of GPS/IMU, force plates, commercial biomechanics, systematic reviews, and unfiltered social media.
- From 2020 the field is defined by scale, integration, and scrutiny rather than new science. Journals have more than doubled since 1990. By 2026 the constraint is not lack of information but vetting, filtering, and integrating it. AI is good for preliminary research and accelerating skilled coders, bad for oversimplification (one-page summaries of books, staff handing in ChatGPT reviews), and ugly when used to generate annual plans, rehab programs, or strength programs by people without the underlying skill.
- Part II: many current staff never studied the fundamentals behind what they do and have never worked without GPS or force plates, so equipment is seen as environment rather than tool. Weber's example: asked for a testing structure to integrate athletes, staff replied with a list of devices instead of the capacities they wanted to understand. That is inverse thinking; start with the question, not the equipment.
- People matter because a high-performance tech framework requires three things in staff: knowledge, curiosity, and work ethic. Those feed knowledge and behaviour, the two axes of the matrix. Rogers' innovation adoption curve is used to show how technology adoption moves through a population; higher knowledge and behaviour predicts earlier and more effective adoption (GPS was rejected outright by every code at a 1998 Australian meeting and is now universal).
- Part III applies the matrix grid: a handbrake who is also coasting is a red mark; a pawn who is a catalyst is worth investing in; an operator who is coasting may not help you build an elite team. Special Forces selection is cited: the highest aptitude is not always what you want, you want people who communicate and work in a team.
- The DIKW pyramid (data, information, knowledge, wisdom) frames the goal: move from collecting data to distilling knowledge for a recipient. "Pick-up 52" dashboards dump every card on the floor and make the coach or medical colleague do the interpretation. Start with the question, define equipment and standards, assess from multiple perspectives (one favourable eccentric hamstring number does not equal readiness), and simplify carefully (SpeedSig's classification of 64 back-end data points into one athlete type is his product example).

### Lab 1A: Building a Common Language (transcript plus Lab_1A_Blog PDF)

- Everyone speaks English but not the same language. Coaches, physios, sport scientists, and rehab staff bring different histories and mentors; without a shared framework meetings degrade into arguments about exercises instead of solutions for athletes.
- Means versus modality (from old Russian training literature): means is why (the quality or adaptation you want), modality is what (the drill, exercise, test, or tool). An A-skip is one modality that can serve as a warm-up means or a low-level plyometric means. Once you agree the means you can be flexible on modality.
- Technology comes third, not first: means, then modality, then technology. "Technology is there to measure and guide what matters. It doesn't decide what matters."
- CM² (Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum) is a shared athlete map so anyone on staff can answer "where does this athlete currently live in our model" in one sentence.
- You do not have to use these labels, but you must have something: written down, distributed, and stuck to.

### Lab 1B, Parts 1 and 2: People and Effective Ops (transcripts plus Lab_1b_Blog PDF and Student Workbook)

- Sun Tzu's "know thyself and know thy enemy" reframed: in a performance department the enemy is internal constraints, people who quietly slow things down, knowledge gaps nobody admits, behaviours that do not match the standards on the wall.
- First question for any leader: what could derail this? A 60-second exercise from a colleague: write down the five things that will stop this department from working.
- Leadership is not a badge; aspiring leaders must practice reading themselves and their environment before they get the title.
- Knowledge axis (handbrake, pawn, practitioner, operator) and behaviour axis (misaligned, coaster, catalyst) combine into an ops audit that drives decisions on mentoring, responsibility, and who should not be in the system. Mentors must have worked at the level you aspire to.
- Practical tests of where people sit: ask about their CPD, have them present ten minutes at a staff meeting on what they worked on last month, put them on the spot on technical matters. Transcript-only "politician" archetype: vocal on admin, days off, and allowances, rarely has a voice on technical matters.
- The matrix is a CPD design tool for leaders and an honest self-check for staff, ideally cross-checked with your boss. Misaligned people need to be managed out or away from critical decisions.

### Lab 1C: The Tech Stack Audit (transcript plus Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit PDF; the Free Version is byte-identical)

- Most environments are tech-rich and procedure-poor. The industry confuses brands with tests and outputs ("we're doing NordBord" names a product; the test is eccentric knee flexor strength).
- Step one is an inventory by measurement system, starting with the most overlooked tool: your computer, which most practitioners use like a typewriter. Then wearables (really GNSS plus IMU), force plates (force over time, not jump height machines), force transducers (setup change equals test change), and linear position transducers (only useful with naming, setup, ROM, valid-rep, and reporting rules standardised).
- Step two is reliability: can you repeat the number within a small error band, within session and between sessions? Published reliability matters; in-house reliability matters more because your staff, setup, and athletes create your real-world error.
- Step three is procedures: the hidden multiplier and your professional IP. Warm-up, familiarisation, instructions, and trials locked and part of onboarding. A leader should be able to walk into any environment and say "these are our procedures, this is our starting point."
- Discipline breeds freedom (Willink). Do not buy new tech; order the tech you have and earn the right to trust it.

### Podcast 1: The False Promise of Technology without Discipline (transcript plus False_Promise blog PDF; Free Version byte-identical)

- Tools do not create clarity; discipline does. Buying a tool and collecting data does not automatically improve performance. Without discipline you get more data, more noise, more arguments, and less trust.
- Discipline means repeatable behaviour: standardised protocols, correct maths and statistics, consistent operations. Missing any one turns the tool into a random number generator.
- Three failure modes: protocol drift, statistics-free interpretation, communication chaos.
- Three disciplines: protocol (earn the right to compare), critical maths (do not confuse noise for change; "sports astrology"), communication alignment (shared language, shared procedures, meeting tempo tied to the competition cycle).
- False promise sounds like: "we bought the system so now we have objective truth", "the dashboard says red so we pulled him", "we monitor everything all the time".
- Three closing rules: standardise capture before scaling collection; define real change through local reliability; make decisions the product.

## Frameworks and tools taught

### 1. Means versus Modality, then Technology (Lab 1A)

What it is: a two-word vocabulary that separates purpose from activity, plus a fixed ordering that puts equipment last.

How to run it:
1. For any drill, exercise, or test in a program, ask "what's the means?" (what physical quality or adaptation are we trying to change: strength, stiffness, deceleration, asymmetry, rehab tolerance).
2. Only then discuss the modality (the specific drill, lift, or test) and accept that the same modality can serve different means.
3. Only then ask what technology can evaluate or support that work.
4. In staff meetings, ban "why are you using that drill" and "I don't like that exercise"; replace with "what are you trying to achieve with that drill?"

What it produces: shorter meetings, exercise selection defended by intent, and a habit of choosing tests by question rather than by available kit.

### 2. CM² athlete map: Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum (Lab 1A)

What it is: a four-stage progression model that gives every discipline one sentence to locate an athlete.

Stages:
1. Control: single joints or very simple patterns; regain or establish basic control; early rehab or very low training age. Move through it as fast as possible; do not park athletes in isolated clams and wall balances once they have the basics.
2. Movement: link joints into coordinated, repeatable multi-joint patterns; move viably as a whole system without falling apart.
3. Capacity: volume, tolerance, robustness; build the engine to handle training and competition loads; developing athletes live here for large parts of the year.
4. Maximum: highest intensities (max strength, power, speed); short exposures balanced against capacity; you oscillate between capacity and maximum rather than living in maximum.

How to run it: agree the stage definitions in writing, give every staff member a copy, and use the phrases in every athlete conversation ("she's in a movement-capacity block", "he's not moving well, pull him back to control", "we can't justify maximum work until his capacity improves"). Adapt the labels if you like but keep one shared map.

What it produces: a common athlete-status language that Athletic Medicine, Athletic Performance, and coaches can all use without a fifteen-minute explanation.

### 3. Knowledge-Behaviour Matrix (Webinar Parts II and III, Lab 1B, Student Workbook)

What it is: a grid for auditing yourself and your staff on two independent axes. It evaluates capability and engagement, not personal worth.

Knowledge axis (x-axis, PDF-confirmed):
- Handbrake: does not understand the concepts or tech, may choose not to learn, increases everyone else's workload. Not automatically a bad person, but a bad fit if they stay stuck.
- Pawn: limited knowledge and experience but can execute clearly defined tasks and build momentum; with mentoring can grow into any piece on the board.
- Practitioner: solid professional, understands the space, competent with your technology, has frameworks and operates reliably. The backbone of the department.
- Operator: deep understanding plus broad experience; can design, integrate, and troubleshoot complex systems and see how technology, training, and operations connect.

Behaviour axis (y-axis, PDF-confirmed three levels):
- Misaligned: does not buy the vision, does not care about direction, can actively undermine; eventually moved on or away from critical decisions.
- Coaster: happy to be here, does the minimum, useful in stable routine roles; you can carry one or two but cannot build a department from them.
- Catalyst: creates movement, influences others, does not always have the answer but finds the path; leaders with or without the title. Support, retain, give responsibility.
- (Webinar transcript adds a fourth top level, Beacon: knowledge plus passion to lead professionals across a domain. The PDFs and workbook stop at Catalyst.)

How to run it with staff, following the Student Workbook (sections A to D):
1. A: each person writes their own definitions of the two axes and of all seven categories from memory, then checks against notes.
2. B1: self-place on each axis and write why.
3. B2: list two or three concrete behaviours as evidence for each self-rating.
4. B3: choose a three-to-five-year target on each axis and write what must change.
5. C1: map three to five people you work with above, beside, and below you, using initials or role titles only, with one example each.
6. C2: answer four tech and ops questions: who are the handbrakes with technology, who are the pawns with growth potential, who are the operators you can learn from, who behaves like a catalyst.
7. D1: three concrete actions in the next 30 to 90 days to move one step on either axis.
8. D2: pick one person from the table, name their current position and desired shift, and write specifically what you will do to help.
9. D3 (private): is anyone both handbrake and misaligned; what risk do they pose; what realistic options exist (role change, clearer expectations, eventual exit); what conversations have you been avoiding.
10. D4: complete "If I truly know myself and know my people, the one thing I must do differently over the next three months is..."

Leader-side probes from Lab 1B: ask staff what they are working on for CPD, ask them to present ten minutes at a staff meeting on last month's work, and test technical understanding periodically. Use the matrix to design each person's CPD plan and to sanity-check hires.

What it produces: a written map of the department, a personal development target, a CPD plan per person, and a list of the hard conversations.

### 4. Tech Stack Reality Check (Lab 1C)

What it is: a three-step audit that converts a pile of devices into a set of measurements you can trust.

Step 1, inventory by measurement system (not brand):
- Your computer: what machine and specs, what software beyond spreadsheets, can you run data workflows, dashboards, or basic coding tools when needed.
- Wearables: GNSS plus IMU; know what is measured versus calculated and what assumptions sit under each output. Do not consume black-box metrics.
- Force plates: they measure force over time; understand impulse and time-specific strategies, not one jump-height number. Be able to explain the force-time curve.
- Force transducers and load cells: IMTP, iso squat and lunge, prone hamstring isometrics, eccentric hamstring tasks, dynamometry. A one-degree change in angle or alignment is a different test.
- Linear position transducers: standardise exercise naming, setup position, range-of-motion rules, valid-rep rules, and reporting rules (best rep versus average versus peak).
- Anything else you run (EMG etc.).

Step 2, reliability: for each measurement, can you repeat the number within a small error band, within session and between sessions? Record where the evidence comes from: published data, internal repeat testing, or "we don't know yet".

Step 3, procedures: draft a one-page procedure per tool covering warm-up, familiarisation, instructions, trial count, valid-rep and exclusion rules, reporting rule. Make it part of onboarding.

What it produces: the five-item submission listed under Deliverables, and the department's procedural IP.

### 5. Three failure modes, three disciplines, three rules (Podcast 1)

Failure modes to watch for:
1. Protocol drift: same test name, different warm-up, angle, or execution; leaders who are not present must be able to trust the result.
2. Statistics-free interpretation: "he's improved, she's worse" with no grasp of change relative to device accuracy.
3. Communication chaos: dashboards exist but decisions are ad hoc, information is not aligned, actions are not assigned.

Disciplines that close the gap:
1. Protocol: earn the right to compare. Lock down what the test is and what it is not, define valid reps and exclusions, standardise steps and instructions. Protects staff, supports onboarding, protects athletes from false conclusions.
2. Critical maths: every signal has information and noise. Establish system reliability (ICC, standard error of measurement, across different testers) and set thresholds for meaningful change. If you cannot explain why you trust the change, you cannot ask anyone to act on it.
3. Communication alignment: align language and procedures, and use consistent meeting structures that give the week a tempo and checkpoints tied to the competition cycle (whether a 14-day or 3-day lead-in).

Closing rules: standardise data capture before scaling collection; define real change by understanding reliability in your environment; make decisions the product.

### 6. Transcript-only concepts worth keeping

- DIKW pyramid: transform data to information, distill information to knowledge, communicate knowledge toward wisdom. Aim for the top of the pyramid in every report.
- Pick-up 52: the dashboard that drops all 52 cards and makes the coach sort them. Because you can build a visualisation does not mean you should.
- Rogers adoption curve: innovators, early adopters, early and late majority, laggards; use it to judge where a technology sits and where your people sit relative to it.
- Five things that will derail us: 60-second leadership quiz.
- Politician archetype: vocal on admin, silent on technical matters; test with a technical presentation.

## Deliverables / exercises

1. Common language document (Lab 1A): write down the shared vocabulary (means versus modality) and a program framework (CM² or your own), give every staff member a copy, and hold to it.
2. Five-things-that-will-derail-us list (Lab 1B Part 1, transcript-only): 60 seconds, write the five internal threats to the department.
3. Knowledge-Behaviour Profile Student Worksheet (Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook.pdf, five pages, sections A to D): definitions, self-audit with evidence, 3 to 5 year target, map of 3 to 5 people, tech and ops impact questions, 30 to 90 day personal actions, one person to develop, private hard-decision reflection, final sentence.
4. Tech Stack Reality Check submission (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.4):
   - List your tech stack grouped by measurement system, not brand.
   - For each tool, one line on what it truly measures (raw signal).
   - For each tool, one line on what you currently report (derived metrics).
   - For each tool, where reliability evidence comes from: published data, internal repeat testing, or "we don't know yet".
   - Pick one tool and draft a one-page procedure for it.
5. Implicit from the podcast: define, in writing, what real change means for each measurement in your environment before scaling collection.

## Key quotes

1. "Technology is there to measure and guide what matters. It doesn't decide what matters." (Lab_1A_Blog PDF p.2)
2. "Once we agree on the means, we can be flexible with modality." (Lab_1A_Blog PDF p.1)
3. "You don't have to use those exact labels. But you do need something." (Lab_1A_Blog PDF p.3)
4. "No amount of software, dashboards or hardware will compensate for persistent handbrakes or misaligned staff." (Lab_1b_Blog PDF p.3)
5. "Many environments are tech-rich and procedure-poor." (Lab_1c PDF p.1)
6. "NordBord is a product. The test is eccentric knee flexor strength. If you confuse the two, you'll eventually confuse your results as well." (Lab_1c PDF p.1)
7. "If your setup changes, your test changes." (Lab_1c PDF p.2)
8. "You'll chase noise and call it insight." (Lab_1c PDF p.3)
9. "The device doesn't create trust. Your procedure does." (Lab_1c PDF p.3)
10. "Discipline gives you reliability. Reliability gives you confidence. Confidence gives you decisions you can actually act on." (Lab_1c PDF p.4)
11. "Earn the right to compare. If you can't repeat it, you can't learn from it." (False_Promise PDF p.1; Podcast 1 approx 04:24)
12. "The tool is not the upgrade, discipline is." (False_Promise PDF p.2; Podcast 1 approx 09:36)
13. "It's not about R or Python or how funky you can make things. It's about what problem are you trying to solve for the person you're communicating to." (Webinar Part III approx 06:21, transcript-only)
14. "Don't sweat about buying new tech, order the tech you already have, and then earn the right to trust it." (Lab 1C approx 05:54, transcript-only)

## Source confidence

PDF extraction status (all five extracted full text; none were image-only):
- Lab_1A_Blog_Building_a_Common_Language.pdf: 3 pages, © Old Bull Performance 2026, titled "Data to Decisions Lab 1a Blog".
- Lab_1b_Blog_Know_Yourself_Know_Your_People.pdf: 4 pages, © Old Bull Performance 2026.

# Module 1: People, Language, and Discipline Before Technology

Module 1 argues that the performance industry has spent the last fifteen years buying technology faster than it has built the people, shared language, and procedures needed to use it. Jason Weber (Old Bull Performance, creator of SpeedSig) traces the field from Milo of Croton to machine learning to show that the constraint is no longer access to information or equipment; it is vetting, filtering, and integrating what you already have. The module's fix has three layers: audit your people on a knowledge and behaviour matrix, agree a common language so cross-discipline staff can locate an athlete and a purpose in seconds, and inventory your tech stack by measurement system so you know what each device actually measures and whether you can repeat the number. The recurring principle is that discipline breeds freedom: standardised procedures produce reliability, reliability produces confidence, and confidence produces decisions you can defend. Every piece of equipment is a tool that must sit inside an operating system; the tool is not the upgrade, the discipline is.

## Lessons

### Webinar 1, Parts I to III: From Milo to Machine Learning (transcript-only, speaker unnamed but consistent with Weber)

- Part I is a history: Milo's calf as progressive overload; 1950s to 1970s birth of modern sport science (USSR institutes, Matveyev's periodisation, Verkhoshansky's shock method, VO2max work); 1970s to 1990s institutes and specialisation (AIS, Ball State biomechanics, Holloszy and Costill); 1990s explosion of injury epidemiology, EMG, 3D motion analysis, plus a second stream of coach-sourced information (Poliquin, King, Chek); 2000 to 2020 the "technology quickening" of GPS/IMU, force plates, commercial biomechanics, systematic reviews, and unfiltered social media.
- From 2020 the field is defined by scale, integration, and scrutiny rather than new science. Journals have more than doubled since 1990. By 2026 the constraint is not lack of information but vetting, filtering, and integrating it. AI is good for preliminary research and accelerating skilled coders, bad for oversimplification (one-page summaries of books, staff handing in ChatGPT reviews), and ugly when used to generate annual plans, rehab programs, or strength programs by people without the underlying skill.
- Part II: many current staff never studied the fundamentals behind what they do and have never worked without GPS or force plates, so equipment is seen as environment rather than tool. Weber's example: asked for a testing structure to integrate athletes, staff replied with a list of devices instead of the capacities they wanted to understand. That is inverse thinking; start with the question, not the equipment.
- People matter because a high-performance tech framework requires three things in staff: knowledge, curiosity, and work ethic. Those feed knowledge and behaviour, the two axes of the matrix. Rogers' innovation adoption curve is used to show how technology adoption moves through a population; higher knowledge and behaviour predicts earlier and more effective adoption (GPS was rejected outright by every code at a 1998 Australian meeting and is now universal).
- Part III applies the matrix grid: a handbrake who is also coasting is a red mark; a pawn who is a catalyst is worth investing in; an operator who is coasting may not help you build an elite team. Special Forces selection is cited: the highest aptitude is not always what you want, you want people who communicate and work in a team.
- The DIKW pyramid (data, information, knowledge, wisdom) frames the goal: move from collecting data to distilling knowledge for a recipient. "Pick-up 52" dashboards dump every card on the floor and make the coach or medical colleague do the interpretation. Start with the question, define equipment and standards, assess from multiple perspectives (one favourable eccentric hamstring number does not equal readiness), and simplify carefully (SpeedSig's classification of 64 back-end data points into one athlete type is his product example).

### Lab 1A: Building a Common Language (transcript plus Lab_1A_Blog PDF)

- Everyone speaks English but not the same language. Coaches, physios, sport scientists, and rehab staff bring different histories and mentors; without a shared framework meetings degrade into arguments about exercises instead of solutions for athletes.
- Means versus modality (from old Russian training literature): means is why (the quality or adaptation you want), modality is what (the drill, exercise, test, or tool). An A-skip is one modality that can serve as a warm-up means or a low-level plyometric means. Once you agree the means you can be flexible on modality.
- Technology comes third, not first: means, then modality, then technology. "Technology is there to measure and guide what matters. It doesn't decide what matters."
- CM² (Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum) is a shared athlete map so anyone on staff can answer "where does this athlete currently live in our model" in one sentence.
- You do not have to use these labels, but you must have something: written down, distributed, and stuck to.

### Lab 1B, Parts 1 and 2: People and Effective Ops (transcripts plus Lab_1b_Blog PDF and Student Workbook)

- Sun Tzu's "know thyself and know thy enemy" reframed: in a performance department the enemy is internal constraints, people who quietly slow things down, knowledge gaps nobody admits, behaviours that do not match the standards on the wall.
- First question for any leader: what could derail this? A 60-second exercise from a colleague: write down the five things that will stop this department from working.
- Leadership is not a badge; aspiring leaders must practice reading themselves and their environment before they get the title.
- Knowledge axis (handbrake, pawn, practitioner, operator) and behaviour axis (misaligned, coaster, catalyst) combine into an ops audit that drives decisions on mentoring, responsibility, and who should not be in the system. Mentors must have worked at the level you aspire to.
- Practical tests of where people sit: ask about their CPD, have them present ten minutes at a staff meeting on what they worked on last month, put them on the spot on technical matters. Transcript-only "politician" archetype: vocal on admin, days off, and allowances, rarely has a voice on technical matters.
- The matrix is a CPD design tool for leaders and an honest self-check for staff, ideally cross-checked with your boss. Misaligned people need to be managed out or away from critical decisions.

### Lab 1C: The Tech Stack Audit (transcript plus Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit PDF; the Free Version is byte-identical)

- Most environments are tech-rich and procedure-poor. The industry confuses brands with tests and outputs ("we're doing NordBord" names a product; the test is eccentric knee flexor strength).
- Step one is an inventory by measurement system, starting with the most overlooked tool: your computer, which most practitioners use like a typewriter. Then wearables (really GNSS plus IMU), force plates (force over time, not jump height machines), force transducers (setup change equals test change), and linear position transducers (only useful with naming, setup, ROM, valid-rep, and reporting rules standardised).
- Step two is reliability: can you repeat the number within a small error band, within session and between sessions? Published reliability matters; in-house reliability matters more because your staff, setup, and athletes create your real-world error.
- Step three is procedures: the hidden multiplier and your professional IP. Warm-up, familiarisation, instructions, and trials locked and part of onboarding. A leader should be able to walk into any environment and say "these are our procedures, this is our starting point."
- Discipline breeds freedom (Willink). Do not buy new tech; order the tech you have and earn the right to trust it.

### Podcast 1: The False Promise of Technology without Discipline (transcript plus False_Promise blog PDF; Free Version byte-identical)

- Tools do not create clarity; discipline does. Buying a tool and collecting data does not automatically improve performance. Without discipline you get more data, more noise, more arguments, and less trust.
- Discipline means repeatable behaviour: standardised protocols, correct maths and statistics, consistent operations. Missing any one turns the tool into a random number generator.
- Three failure modes: protocol drift, statistics-free interpretation, communication chaos.
- Three disciplines: protocol (earn the right to compare), critical maths (do not confuse noise for change; "sports astrology"), communication alignment (shared language, shared procedures, meeting tempo tied to the competition cycle).
- False promise sounds like: "we bought the system so now we have objective truth", "the dashboard says red so we pulled him", "we monitor everything all the time".
- Three closing rules: standardise capture before scaling collection; define real change through local reliability; make decisions the product.

## Frameworks and tools taught

### 1. Means versus Modality, then Technology (Lab 1A)

What it is: a two-word vocabulary that separates purpose from activity, plus a fixed ordering that puts equipment last.

How to run it:
1. For any drill, exercise, or test in a program, ask "what's the means?" (what physical quality or adaptation are we trying to change: strength, stiffness, deceleration, asymmetry, rehab tolerance).
2. Only then discuss the modality (the specific drill, lift, or test) and accept that the same modality can serve different means.
3. Only then ask what technology can evaluate or support that work.
4. In staff meetings, ban "why are you using that drill" and "I don't like that exercise"; replace with "what are you trying to achieve with that drill?"

What it produces: shorter meetings, exercise selection defended by intent, and a habit of choosing tests by question rather than by available kit.

### 2. CM² athlete map: Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum (Lab 1A)

What it is: a four-stage progression model that gives every discipline one sentence to locate an athlete.

Stages:
1. Control: single joints or very simple patterns; regain or establish basic control; early rehab or very low training age. Move through it as fast as possible; do not park athletes in isolated clams and wall balances once they have the basics.
2. Movement: link joints into coordinated, repeatable multi-joint patterns; move viably as a whole system without falling apart.
3. Capacity: volume, tolerance, robustness; build the engine to handle training and competition loads; developing athletes live here for large parts of the year.
4. Maximum: highest intensities (max strength, power, speed); short exposures balanced against capacity; you oscillate between capacity and maximum rather than living in maximum.

How to run it: agree the stage definitions in writing, give every staff member a copy, and use the phrases in every athlete conversation ("she's in a movement-capacity block", "he's not moving well, pull him back to control", "we can't justify maximum work until his capacity improves"). Adapt the labels if you like but keep one shared map.

What it produces: a common athlete-status language that Athletic Medicine, Athletic Performance, and coaches can all use without a fifteen-minute explanation.

### 3. Knowledge-Behaviour Matrix (Webinar Parts II and III, Lab 1B, Student Workbook)

What it is: a grid for auditing yourself and your staff on two independent axes. It evaluates capability and engagement, not personal worth.

Knowledge axis (x-axis, PDF-confirmed):
- Handbrake: does not understand the concepts or tech, may choose not to learn, increases everyone else's workload. Not automatically a bad person, but a bad fit if they stay stuck.
- Pawn: limited knowledge and experience but can execute clearly defined tasks and build momentum; with mentoring can grow into any piece on the board.
- Practitioner: solid professional, understands the space, competent with your technology, has frameworks and operates reliably. The backbone of the department.
- Operator: deep understanding plus broad experience; can design, integrate, and troubleshoot complex systems and see how technology, training, and operations connect.

Behaviour axis (y-axis, PDF-confirmed three levels):
- Misaligned: does not buy the vision, does not care about direction, can actively undermine; eventually moved on or away from critical decisions.
- Coaster: happy to be here, does the minimum, useful in stable routine roles; you can carry one or two but cannot build a department from them.
- Catalyst: creates movement, influences others, does not always have the answer but finds the path; leaders with or without the title. Support, retain, give responsibility.
- (Webinar transcript adds a fourth top level, Beacon: knowledge plus passion to lead professionals across a domain. The PDFs and workbook stop at Catalyst.)

How to run it with staff, following the Student Workbook (sections A to D):
1. A: each person writes their own definitions of the two axes and of all seven categories from memory, then checks against notes.
2. B1: self-place on each axis and write why.
3. B2: list two or three concrete behaviours as evidence for each self-rating.
4. B3: choose a three-to-five-year target on each axis and write what must change.
5. C1: map three to five people you work with above, beside, and below you, using initials or role titles only, with one example each.
6. C2: answer four tech and ops questions: who are the handbrakes with technology, who are the pawns with growth potential, who are the operators you can learn from, who behaves like a catalyst.
7. D1: three concrete actions in the next 30 to 90 days to move one step on either axis.
8. D2: pick one person from the table, name their current position and desired shift, and write specifically what you will do to help.
9. D3 (private): is anyone both handbrake and misaligned; what risk do they pose; what realistic options exist (role change, clearer expectations, eventual exit); what conversations have you been avoiding.
10. D4: complete "If I truly know myself and know my people, the one thing I must do differently over the next three months is..."

Leader-side probes from Lab 1B: ask staff what they are working on for CPD, ask them to present ten minutes at a staff meeting on last month's work, and test technical understanding periodically. Use the matrix to design each person's CPD plan and to sanity-check hires.

What it produces: a written map of the department, a personal development target, a CPD plan per person, and a list of the hard conversations.

### 4. Tech Stack Reality Check (Lab 1C)

What it is: a three-step audit that converts a pile of devices into a set of measurements you can trust.

Step 1, inventory by measurement system (not brand):
- Your computer: what machine and specs, what software beyond spreadsheets, can you run data workflows, dashboards, or basic coding tools when needed.
- Wearables: GNSS plus IMU; know what is measured versus calculated and what assumptions sit under each output. Do not consume black-box metrics.
- Force plates: they measure force over time; understand impulse and time-specific strategies, not one jump-height number. Be able to explain the force-time curve.
- Force transducers and load cells: IMTP, iso squat and lunge, prone hamstring isometrics, eccentric hamstring tasks, dynamometry. A one-degree change in angle or alignment is a different test.
- Linear position transducers: standardise exercise naming, setup position, range-of-motion rules, valid-rep rules, and reporting rules (best rep versus average versus peak).
- Anything else you run (EMG etc.).

Step 2, reliability: for each measurement, can you repeat the number within a small error band, within session and between sessions? Record where the evidence comes from: published data, internal repeat testing, or "we don't know yet".

Step 3, procedures: draft a one-page procedure per tool covering warm-up, familiarisation, instructions, trial count, valid-rep and exclusion rules, reporting rule. Make it part of onboarding.

What it produces: the five-item submission listed under Deliverables, and the department's procedural IP.

### 5. Three failure modes, three disciplines, three rules (Podcast 1)

Failure modes to watch for:
1. Protocol drift: same test name, different warm-up, angle, or execution; leaders who are not present must be able to trust the result.
2. Statistics-free interpretation: "he's improved, she's worse" with no grasp of change relative to device accuracy.
3. Communication chaos: dashboards exist but decisions are ad hoc, information is not aligned, actions are not assigned.

Disciplines that close the gap:
1. Protocol: earn the right to compare. Lock down what the test is and what it is not, define valid reps and exclusions, standardise steps and instructions. Protects staff, supports onboarding, protects athletes from false conclusions.
2. Critical maths: every signal has information and noise. Establish system reliability (ICC, standard error of measurement, across different testers) and set thresholds for meaningful change. If you cannot explain why you trust the change, you cannot ask anyone to act on it.
3. Communication alignment: align language and procedures, and use consistent meeting structures that give the week a tempo and checkpoints tied to the competition cycle (whether a 14-day or 3-day lead-in).

Closing rules: standardise data capture before scaling collection; define real change by understanding reliability in your environment; make decisions the product.

- DIKW pyramid: transform data to information, distill information to knowledge, communicate knowledge toward wisdom. Aim for the top of the pyramid in every report.
- Pick-up 52: the dashboard that drops all 52 cards and makes the coach sort them. Because you can build a visualisation does not mean you should.
- Rogers adoption curve: innovators, early adopters, early and late majority, laggards; use it to judge where a technology sits and where your people sit relative to it.
- Five things that will derail us: 60-second leadership quiz.
- Politician archetype: vocal on admin, silent on technical matters; test with a technical presentation.

## Deliverables / exercises

1. Common language document (Lab 1A): write down the shared vocabulary (means versus modality) and a program framework (CM² or your own), give every staff member a copy, and hold to it.
2. Five-things-that-will-derail-us list (Lab 1B Part 1, transcript-only): 60 seconds, write the five internal threats to the department.
3. Knowledge-Behaviour Profile Student Worksheet (Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook.pdf, five pages, sections A to D): definitions, self-audit with evidence, 3 to 5 year target, map of 3 to 5 people, tech and ops impact questions, 30 to 90 day personal actions, one person to develop, private hard-decision reflection, final sentence.
4. Tech Stack Reality Check submission (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.4):
   - List your tech stack grouped by measurement system, not brand.
   - For each tool, one line on what it truly measures (raw signal).
   - For each tool, one line on what you currently report (derived metrics).
   - For each tool, where reliability evidence comes from: published data, internal repeat testing, or "we don't know yet".
   - Pick one tool and draft a one-page procedure for it.
5. Implicit from the podcast: define, in writing, what real change means for each measurement in your environment before scaling collection.

## Key quotes

1. "Technology is there to measure and guide what matters. It doesn't decide what matters." (Lab_1A_Blog PDF p.2)
2. "Once we agree on the means, we can be flexible with modality." (Lab_1A_Blog PDF p.1)
3. "You don't have to use those exact labels. But you do need something." (Lab_1A_Blog PDF p.3)
4. "No amount of software, dashboards or hardware will compensate for persistent handbrakes or misaligned staff." (Lab_1b_Blog PDF p.3)
5. "Many environments are tech-rich and procedure-poor." (Lab_1c PDF p.1)
6. "NordBord is a product. The test is eccentric knee flexor strength. If you confuse the two, you'll eventually confuse your results as well." (Lab_1c PDF p.1)
7. "If your setup changes, your test changes." (Lab_1c PDF p.2)
8. "You'll chase noise and call it insight." (Lab_1c PDF p.3)
9. "The device doesn't create trust. Your procedure does." (Lab_1c PDF p.3)
10. "Discipline gives you reliability. Reliability gives you confidence. Confidence gives you decisions you can actually act on." (Lab_1c PDF p.4)
11. "Earn the right to compare. If you can't repeat it, you can't learn from it." (False_Promise PDF p.1; Podcast 1 approx 04:24)
12. "The tool is not the upgrade, discipline is." (False_Promise PDF p.2; Podcast 1 approx 09:36)
13. "It's not about R or Python or how funky you can make things. It's about what problem are you trying to solve for the person you're communicating to." (Webinar Part III approx 06:21, transcript-only)
14. "Don't sweat about buying new tech, order the tech you already have, and then earn the right to trust it." (Lab 1C approx 05:54, transcript-only)

An A-skip is one modality that can serve as a warm-up means or a low-level plyometric means. Once you agree the means you can be flexible on modality.
- Technology comes third, not first: means, then modality, then technology. "Technology is there to measure and guide what matters. It doesn't decide what matters."
- CM² (Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum) is a shared athlete map so anyone on staff can answer "where does this athlete currently live in our model" in one sentence.
- You do not have to use these labels, but you must have something: written down, distributed, and stuck to.

### Lab 1B, Parts 1 and 2: People and Effective Ops (transcripts plus Lab_1b_Blog PDF and Student Workbook)

- Sun Tzu's "know thyself and know thy enemy" reframed: in a performance department the enemy is internal constraints, people who quietly slow things down, knowledge gaps nobody admits, behaviours that do not match the standards on the wall.
- First question for any leader: what could derail this? A 60-second exercise from a colleague: write down the five things that will stop this department from working.
- Leadership is not a badge; aspiring leaders must practice reading themselves and their environment before they get the title.
- Knowledge axis (handbrake, pawn, practitioner, operator) and behaviour axis (misaligned, coaster, catalyst) combine into an ops audit that drives decisions on mentoring, responsibility, and who should not be in the system. Mentors must have worked at the level you aspire to.
- Practical tests of where people sit: ask about their CPD, have them present ten minutes at a staff meeting on what they worked on last month, put them on the spot on technical matters. Transcript-only "politician" archetype: vocal on admin, days off, and allowances, rarely has a voice on technical matters.
- The matrix is a CPD design tool for leaders and an honest self-check for staff, ideally cross-checked with your boss. Misaligned people need to be managed out or away from critical decisions.

### Lab 1C: The Tech Stack Audit (transcript plus Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit PDF; the Free Version is byte-identical)

- Most environments are tech-rich and procedure-poor. The industry confuses brands with tests and outputs ("we're doing NordBord" names a product; the test is eccentric knee flexor strength).
- Step one is an inventory by measurement system, starting with the most overlooked tool: your computer, which most practitioners use like a typewriter. Then wearables (really GNSS plus IMU), force plates (force over time, not jump height machines), force transducers (setup change equals test change), and linear position transducers (only useful with naming, setup, ROM, valid-rep, and reporting rules standardised).
- Step two is reliability: can you repeat the number within a small error band, within session and between sessions? Published reliability matters; in-house reliability matters more because your staff, setup, and athletes create your real-world error.
- Step three is procedures: the hidden multiplier and your professional IP. Warm-up, familiarisation, instructions, and trials locked and part of onboarding. A leader should be able to walk into any environment and say "these are our procedures, this is our starting point."
- Discipline breeds freedom (Willink). Do not buy new tech; order the tech you have and earn the right to trust it.

### Podcast 1: The False Promise of Technology without Discipline (transcript plus False_Promise blog PDF; Free Version byte-identical)

- Tools do not create clarity; discipline does. Buying a tool and collecting data does not automatically improve performance. Without discipline you get more data, more noise, more arguments, and less trust.
- Discipline means repeatable behaviour: standardised protocols, correct maths and statistics, consistent operations. Missing any one turns the tool into a random number generator.
- Three failure modes: protocol drift, statistics-free interpretation, communication chaos.
- Three disciplines: protocol (earn the right to compare), critical maths (do not confuse noise for change; "sports astrology"), communication alignment (shared language, shared procedures, meeting tempo tied to the competition cycle).
- False promise sounds like: "we bought the system so now we have objective truth", "the dashboard says red so we pulled him", "we monitor everything all the time".
- Three closing rules: standardise capture before scaling collection; define real change through local reliability; make decisions the product.

## Frameworks and tools taught

### 1. Means versus Modality, then Technology (Lab 1A)

What it is: a two-word vocabulary that separates purpose from activity, plus a fixed ordering that puts equipment last.

How to run it:
1. For any drill, exercise, or test in a program, ask "what's the means?" (what physical quality or adaptation are we trying to change: strength, stiffness, deceleration, asymmetry, rehab tolerance).
2. Only then discuss the modality (the specific drill, lift, or test) and accept that the same modality can serve different means.
3. Only then ask what technology can evaluate or support that work.
4. In staff meetings, ban "why are you using that drill" and "I don't like that exercise"; replace with "what are you trying to achieve with that drill?"

What it produces: shorter meetings, exercise selection defended by intent, and a habit of choosing tests by question rather than by available kit.

### 2. CM² athlete map: Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum (Lab 1A)

What it is: a four-stage progression model that gives every discipline one sentence to locate an athlete.

Stages:
1. Control: single joints or very simple patterns; regain or establish basic control; early rehab or very low training age. Move through it as fast as possible; do not park athletes in isolated clams and wall balances once they have the basics.
2. Movement: link joints into coordinated, repeatable multi-joint patterns; move viably as a whole system without falling apart.
3. Capacity: volume, tolerance, robustness; build the engine to handle training and competition loads; developing athletes live here for large parts of the year.
4. Maximum: highest intensities (max strength, power, speed); short exposures balanced against capacity; you oscillate between capacity and maximum rather than living in maximum.

How to run it: agree the stage definitions in writing, give every staff member a copy, and use the phrases in every athlete conversation ("she's in a movement-capacity block", "he's not moving well, pull him back to control", "we can't justify maximum work until his capacity improves"). Adapt the labels if you like but keep one shared map.

What it produces: a common athlete-status language that Athletic Medicine, Athletic Performance, and coaches can all use without a fifteen-minute explanation.

### 3. Knowledge-Behaviour Matrix (Webinar Parts II and III, Lab 1B, Student Workbook)

What it is: a grid for auditing yourself and your staff on two independent axes. It evaluates capability and engagement, not personal worth.

Knowledge axis (x-axis, PDF-confirmed):
- Handbrake: does not understand the concepts or tech, may choose not to learn, increases everyone else's workload. Not automatically a bad person, but a bad fit if they stay stuck.
- Pawn: limited knowledge and experience but can execute clearly defined tasks and build momentum; with mentoring can grow into any piece on the board.
- Practitioner: solid professional, understands the space, competent with your technology, has frameworks and operates reliably. The backbone of the department.
- Operator: deep understanding plus broad experience; can design, integrate, and troubleshoot complex systems and see how technology, training, and operations connect.

Behaviour axis (y-axis, PDF-confirmed three levels):
- Misaligned: does not buy the vision, does not care about direction, can actively undermine; eventually moved on or away from critical decisions.
- Coaster: happy to be here, does the minimum, useful in stable routine roles; you can carry one or two but cannot build a department from them.
- Catalyst: creates movement, influences others, does not always have the answer but finds the path; leaders with or without the title. Support, retain, give responsibility.
- (Webinar transcript adds a fourth top level, Beacon: knowledge plus passion to lead professionals across a domain. The PDFs and workbook stop at Catalyst.)

How to run it with staff, following the Student Workbook (sections A to D):
1. A: each person writes their own definitions of the two axes and of all seven categories from memory, then checks against notes.
2. B1: self-place on each axis and write why.
3. B2: list two or three concrete behaviours as evidence for each self-rating.
4. B3: choose a three-to-five-year target on each axis and write what must change.
5. C1: map three to five people you work with above, beside, and below you, using initials or role titles only, with one example each.
6. C2: answer four tech and ops questions: who are the handbrakes with technology, who are the pawns with growth potential, who are the operators you can learn from, who behaves like a catalyst.
7. D1: three concrete actions in the next 30 to 90 days to move one step on either axis.
8. D2: pick one person from the table, name their current position and desired shift, and write specifically what you will do to help.
9. D3 (private): is anyone both handbrake and misaligned; what risk do they pose; what realistic options exist (role change, clearer expectations, eventual exit); what conversations have you been avoiding.
10. D4: complete "If I truly know myself and know my people, the one thing I must do differently over the next three months is..."

Leader-side probes from Lab 1B: ask staff what they are working on for CPD, ask them to present ten minutes at a staff meeting on last month's work, and test technical understanding periodically. Use the matrix to design each person's CPD plan and to sanity-check hires.

What it produces: a written map of the department, a personal development target, a CPD plan per person, and a list of the hard conversations.

### 4. Tech Stack Reality Check (Lab 1C)

What it is: a three-step audit that converts a pile of devices into a set of measurements you can trust.

Step 1, inventory by measurement system (not brand):
- Your computer: what machine and specs, what software beyond spreadsheets, can you run data workflows, dashboards, or basic coding tools when needed.
- Wearables: GNSS plus IMU; know what is measured versus calculated and what assumptions sit under each output. Do not consume black-box metrics.
- Force plates: they measure force over time; understand impulse and time-specific strategies, not one jump-height number. Be able to explain the force-time curve.
- Force transducers and load cells: IMTP, iso squat and lunge, prone hamstring isometrics, eccentric hamstring tasks, dynamometry. A one-degree change in angle or alignment is a different test.
- Linear position transducers: standardise exercise naming, setup position, range-of-motion rules, valid-rep rules, and reporting rules (best rep versus average versus peak).
- Anything else you run (EMG etc.).

Step 2, reliability: for each measurement, can you repeat the number within a small error band, within session and between sessions? Record where the evidence comes from: published data, internal repeat testing, or "we don't know yet".

Step 3, procedures: draft a one-page procedure per tool covering warm-up, familiarisation, instructions, trial count, valid-rep and exclusion rules, reporting rule. Make it part of onboarding.

What it produces: the five-item submission listed under Deliverables, and the department's procedural IP.

### 5. Three failure modes, three disciplines, three rules (Podcast 1)

Failure modes to watch for:
1. Protocol drift: same test name, different warm-up, angle, or execution; leaders who are not present must be able to trust the result.
2. Statistics-free interpretation: "he's improved, she's worse" with no grasp of change relative to device accuracy.
3. Communication chaos: dashboards exist but decisions are ad hoc, information is not aligned, actions are not assigned.

Disciplines that close the gap:
1. Protocol: earn the right to compare. Lock down what the test is and what it is not, define valid reps and exclusions, standardise steps and instructions. Protects staff, supports onboarding, protects athletes from false conclusions.
2. Critical maths: every signal has information and noise. Establish system reliability (ICC, standard error of measurement, across different testers) and set thresholds for meaningful change. If you cannot explain why you trust the change, you cannot ask anyone to act on it.
3. Communication alignment: align language and procedures, and use consistent meeting structures that give the week a tempo and checkpoints tied to the competition cycle (whether a 14-day or 3-day lead-in).

Closing rules: standardise data capture before scaling collection; define real change by understanding reliability in your environment; make decisions the product.

### 6. Transcript-only concepts worth keeping

- DIKW pyramid: transform data to information, distill information to knowledge, communicate knowledge toward wisdom. Aim for the top of the pyramid in every report.
- Pick-up 52: the dashboard that drops all 52 cards and makes the coach sort them. Because you can build a visualisation does not mean you should.
- Rogers adoption curve: innovators, early adopters, early and late majority, laggards; use it to judge where a technology sits and where your people sit relative to it.
- Five things that will derail us: 60-second leadership quiz.
- Politician archetype: vocal on admin, silent on technical matters; test with a technical presentation.

## Deliverables / exercises

1. Common language document (Lab 1A): write down the shared vocabulary (means versus modality) and a program framework (CM² or your own), give every staff member a copy, and hold to it.
2. Five-things-that-will-derail-us list (Lab 1B Part 1, transcript-only): 60 seconds, write the five internal threats to the department.
3. Knowledge-Behaviour Profile Student Worksheet (Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook.pdf, five pages, sections A to D): definitions, self-audit with evidence, 3 to 5 year target, map of 3 to 5 people, tech and ops impact questions, 30 to 90 day personal actions, one person to develop, private hard-decision reflection, final sentence.
4. Tech Stack Reality Check submission (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.4):
   - List your tech stack grouped by measurement system, not brand.
   - For each tool, one line on what it truly measures (raw signal).
   - For each tool, one line on what you currently report (derived metrics).
   - For each tool, where reliability evidence comes from: published data, internal repeat testing, or "we don't know yet".
   - Pick one tool and draft a one-page procedure for it.
5. Implicit from the podcast: define, in writing, what real change means for each measurement in your environment before scaling collection.

## Key quotes

1. "Technology is there to measure and guide what matters. It doesn't decide what matters." (Lab_1A_Blog PDF p.2)
2. "Once we agree on the means, we can be flexible with modality." (Lab_1A_Blog PDF p.1)
3. "You don't have to use those exact labels. But you do need something." (Lab_1A_Blog PDF p.3)
4. "No amount of software, dashboards or hardware will compensate for persistent handbrakes or misaligned staff." (Lab_1b_Blog PDF p.3)
5. "Many environments are tech-rich and procedure-poor." (Lab_1c PDF p.1)
6. "NordBord is a product. The test is eccentric knee flexor strength. If you confuse the two, you'll eventually confuse your results as well." (Lab_1c PDF p.1)
7. "If your setup changes, your test changes." (Lab_1c PDF p.2)
8. "You'll chase noise and call it insight." (Lab_1c PDF p.3)
9. "The device doesn't create trust. Your procedure does." (Lab_1c PDF p.3)
10. "Discipline gives you reliability. Reliability gives you confidence. Confidence gives you decisions you can actually act on." (Lab_1c PDF p.4)
11. "Earn the right to compare. If you can't repeat it, you can't learn from it." (False_Promise PDF p.1; Podcast 1 approx 04:24)
12. "The tool is not the upgrade, discipline is." (False_Promise PDF p.2; Podcast 1 approx 09:36)
13. "It's not about R or Python or how funky you can make things. It's about what problem are you trying to solve for the person you're communicating to." (Webinar Part III approx 06:21, transcript-only)
14. "Don't sweat about buying new tech, order the tech you already have, and then earn the right to trust it." (Lab 1C approx 05:54, transcript-only)

- Part I is a history: Milo's calf as progressive overload; 1950s to 1970s birth of modern sport science (USSR institutes, Matveyev's periodisation, Verkhoshansky's shock method, VO2max work); 1970s to 1990s institutes and specialisation (AIS, Ball State biomechanics, Holloszy and Costill); 1990s explosion of injury epidemiology, EMG, 3D motion analysis, plus a second stream of coach-sourced information (Poliquin, King, Chek); 2000 to 2020 the "technology quickening" of GPS/IMU, force plates, commercial biomechanics, systematic reviews, and unfiltered social media.
- From 2020 the field is defined by scale, integration, and scrutiny rather than new science. Journals have more than doubled since 1990. By 2026 the constraint is not lack of information but vetting, filtering, and integrating it. AI is good for preliminary research and accelerating skilled coders, bad for oversimplification (one-page summaries of books, staff handing in ChatGPT reviews), and ugly when used to generate annual plans, rehab programs, or strength programs by people without the underlying skill.
- Part II: many current staff never studied the fundamentals behind what they do and have never worked without GPS or force plates, so equipment is seen as environment rather than tool. Weber's example: asked for a testing structure to integrate athletes, staff replied with a list of devices instead of the capacities they wanted to understand. That is inverse thinking; start with the question, not the equipment.
- People matter because a high-performance tech framework requires three things in staff: knowledge, curiosity, and work ethic. Those feed knowledge and behaviour, the two axes of the matrix. Rogers' innovation adoption curve is used to show how technology adoption moves through a population; higher knowledge and behaviour predicts earlier and more effective adoption (GPS was rejected outright by every code at a 1998 Australian meeting and is now universal).
- Part III applies the matrix grid: a handbrake who is also coasting is a red mark; a pawn who is a catalyst is worth investing in; an operator who is coasting may not help you build an elite team. Special Forces selection is cited: the highest aptitude is not always what you want, you want people who communicate and work in a team.
- The DIKW pyramid (data, information, knowledge, wisdom) frames the goal: move from collecting data to distilling knowledge for a recipient. "Pick-up 52" dashboards dump every card on the floor and make the coach or medical colleague do the interpretation. Start with the question, define equipment and standards, assess from multiple perspectives (one favourable eccentric hamstring number does not equal readiness), and simplify carefully (SpeedSig's classification of 64 back-end data points into one athlete type is his product example).

input.file_path: C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\RunningTheRoom\notes\module-1.md
input.old_string:
- Everyone speaks English but not the same language. Coaches, physios, sport scientists, and rehab staff bring different histories and mentors; without a shared framework meetings degrade into arguments about exercises instead of solutions for athletes.
- Means versus modality (from old Russian training literature): means is why (the quality or adaptation you want), modality is what (the drill, exercise, test, or tool). An A-skip is one modality that can serve as a warm-up means or a low-level plyometric means. Once you agree the means you can be flexible on modality.
- Technology comes third, not first: means, then modality, then technology. "Technology is there to measure and guide what matters. It doesn't decide what matters."
- CM² (Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum) is a shared athlete map so anyone on staff can answer "where does this athlete currently live in our model" in one sentence.
- You do not have to use these labels, but you must have something: written down, distributed, and stuck to.

### Lab 1B, Parts 1 and 2: People and Effective Ops (transcripts plus Lab_1b_Blog PDF and Student Workbook)

input.file_path: C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\RunningTheRoom\notes\module-1.md
input.old_string:
- Sun Tzu's "know thyself and know thy enemy" reframed: in a performance department the enemy is internal constraints, people who quietly slow things down, knowledge gaps nobody admits, behaviours that do not match the standards on the wall.
- First question for any leader: what could derail this? A 60-second exercise from a colleague: write down the five things that will stop this department from working.
- Leadership is not a badge; aspiring leaders must practice reading themselves and their environment before they get the title.
- Knowledge axis (handbrake, pawn, practitioner, operator) and behaviour axis (misaligned, coaster, catalyst) combine into an ops audit that drives decisions on mentoring, responsibility, and who should not be in the system. Mentors must have worked at the level you aspire to.
- Practical tests of where people sit: ask about their CPD, have them present ten minutes at a staff meeting on what they worked on last month, put them on the spot on technical matters. Transcript-only "politician" archetype: vocal on admin, days off, and allowances, rarely has a voice on technical matters.
- The matrix is a CPD design tool for leaders and an honest self-check for staff, ideally cross-checked with your boss. Misaligned people need to be managed out or away from critical decisions.

### Lab 1C: The Tech Stack Audit (transcript plus Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit PDF; the Free Version is byte-identical)

input.file_path: C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\RunningTheRoom\notes\module-1.md
input.old_string:
- Most environments are tech-rich and procedure-poor. The industry confuses brands with tests and outputs ("we're doing NordBord" names a product; the test is eccentric knee flexor strength).
- Step one is an inventory by measurement system, starting with the most overlooked tool: your computer, which most practitioners use like a typewriter. Then wearables (really GNSS plus IMU), force plates (force over time, not jump height machines), force transducers (setup change equals test change), and linear position transducers (only useful with naming, setup, ROM, valid-rep, and reporting rules standardised).
- Step two is reliability: can you repeat the number within a small error band, within session and between sessions? Published reliability matters; in-house reliability matters more because your staff, setup, and athletes create your real-world error.
- Step three is procedures: the hidden multiplier and your professional IP. Warm-up, familiarisation, instructions, and trials locked and part of onboarding. A leader should be able to walk into any environment and say "these are our procedures, this is our starting point."
- Discipline breeds freedom (Willink). Do not buy new tech; order the tech you have and earn the right to trust it.
